data.title: Canada to Join the NATO Innovation Fund to Advance the Local Defence, Security and Resilience Ecosystem
data.description:
Canada to Join the NATO Innovation Fund to Advance the Local Defence, Security and Resilience Ecosystem

  • Canada becomes the 25th Allied nation to back the NATO Innovation Fund, gaining access to €1.1 billion in mission-aligned capital and a co-investor network spanning the Alliance

Canada announced today it is joining the NATO Innovation Fund, becoming the 25th Allied nation to commit to backing deep tech innovation to address the needs of NATO nations. The Government of Canada is committing EUR 64,590,000 (approximately CAD $100 million) to the firm, with the Business Development Bank of Canada (BDC) holding and managing Canada’s investment in the Fund. This brings total commitments to the NATO Innovation Fund to more than EUR 1.1 billion.

Canadian membership will give domestic innovators access to patient capital, opportunities to accelerate the adoption of their technology by governments and businesses across the Alliance, a large network of co-investors, and lessons learned from the NIF’s work to date across 24 participating nations.

“Canada has the talent, the innovation, and the ambition to be a global leader in defence and security. The NATO Innovation Fund is helping turn that potential into real capabilities by connecting Canadian innovators with the investment and partnerships they need to succeed. This is about strengthening our defence industrial base, supporting the next generation of Canadian companies, and ensuring our Allies have access to the technologies they need to meet the security challenges of tomorrow.” - The Honourable David J. McGuinty, Minister of National Defence

“As Canada’s development bank, BDC has a unique role to play in helping Canadian entrepreneurs build the companies and capabilities our country needs for the future. Our Defence Platform brings together capital, financing, expertise, partnerships and market connections to help defence and dual-use companies move from innovation to commercialization and scale. Canada’s participation in the NATO Innovation Fund extends that reach across the Alliance, giving Canadian entrepreneurs more opportunities to access capital, customers and global supply chains while strengthening Canada’s defence industrial capacity.” - Isabelle Hudon, President and CEO, BDC

"Canada's decision to join the NATO Innovation Fund is a landmark moment – not just for the Fund, but for the Alliance's collective approach to innovation. Canadian innovators will now have access to the Fund’s network of leaders across government, finance, and business, alongside the patient, mission-aligned capital they need to scale. Meanwhile, every one of our participating nations gains something equally valuable: a window into one of the world's most dynamic deep tech ecosystems. That reciprocity – capital and insight flowing in both directions – exemplifies how Allied nations can work together to secure our shared future." - Fiona Murray, Chair of the Board, NATO Innovation Fund

Canada’s accession follows the strong operational and commercial track record of the NIF’s 30+ portfolio companies.

Today’s announcement builds on the strong ties between NIF and Canada, demonstrating how transatlantic collaboration and investment in defence innovation are creating tangible economic and security benefits. Over the past year, NIF portfolio companies have expanded into Canada, including Isar Aerospace, which was selected to develop a launch pad and provide launch services for Canadian satellites, and autonomous airship company Kelluu, which recently entered the Canadian market. These examples highlight how investing in defence innovation can create new business opportunities, attract investment, and drive economic growth on both sides of the Atlantic.

“Canada has a significant opportunity to turn cutting-edge innovation into real-world capabilities that strengthen its defence, security and resilience. Across the Alliance, ambitious startups are developing technologies that governments urgently need. The next step is accelerating their adoption - opening doors to contracts and commercial opportunities for Canadian startups, while giving Canada faster access to the capabilities it needs. This is how we turn investment in innovation into tangible economic and security benefits.” - Ari Jónsson, President, NATO Innovation Fund

Amalia Kontesi

data.title: Micron and Sandisk stocks might look like bargains, but analysts say that's actually a red flag
data.description:
By Hannah Pedone

Cheap valuation multiples for memory stocks have historically been associated with peak pricing levels, according to analysts

Shares of Micron fell nearly 14% on Friday.

Memory stocks were among the biggest decliners as the technology sector bled red ink on Friday.

Shares of Micron Technology (MU) closed down 14% on Friday, while shares of Sandisk (SNDK) fell 16%. Western Digital's stock (WDC) sank 12%.

The pressure on these stocks is mounting. Micron shares are down 50.99% from their peak, while Sandisk shares are down 72.85% from their highs and Western Digital's stock has shed 64.97%.

The chip sector in general has been hit hard due to various factors. Those include concerns that politicians could get stricter about data-center construction, leadership uncertainty at Nvidia (NVDA) and the idea that Anthropic's (ANT) IPO might have sucked attention away from the broader tech sector.

Then there is the perennial debate over the price-to-earnings multiples of memory stocks.

Micron and Sandisk shares both trade at meaningful discounts to their recent historical valuations. Micron's stock trades at 3.76 times estimated earnings for the next 12 months, versus a two-year average of 9.10 times. Sandisk's multiple of 3.04 times forward earnings expectations is below its 10.47-times average since the time of its separation from Western Digital in February 2025.

But Brendan Burke, the research director for semiconductors, supply chain and emerging tech at the Futurum Group, says that low price-to-earnings ratios for memory stocks are a "warning label, not a bargain sign."

"Investors have learned over decades to sell memory stocks at peak earnings, because the earnings side of that ratio has historically collapsed when the cycle turns," he said.

"A multiple in the low single digits tells you the market is pricing today's profits as a peak," he added.

Admittedly, there are some caveats. The historical precedent "ignores that AI has changed the shape of this cycle." Some types of memory, like high-bandwidth memory and solid-state-drive storage, are tied to what he called "mission-critical data-center buildouts," as opposed to memory for PCs and handsets. That distinction means the earnings might be "more durable than these multiples imply," Burke said.

William Blair analyst Sebastien Naji told MarketWatch that there's a limit to the usefulness of low P/E ratios as a "valuation support metric."

Memory stocks often see "extreme volatility in pricing," CreditSights analyst Andy Li added, and that can lead to boom-and-bust cycles.

If investors assume the market is still cyclical, a "dramatic price decline may well be in the cards," he said. "The price action reflects that fear."

Li explained that cyclical stocks like memory often top with "very low" price-to-earnings multiples, because that's when their estimated earnings for the next 12 months are "most inflated." Meanwhile, they also bottom with relatively high multiples, following the same logic, he said.

Separately, he added that the fact that monthly options expire on Friday could also be a technical factor affecting the stocks.

See also: Jensen Huang was a 'China salesman' for Nvidia. His exit is weighing on Chinese tech stocks.

-Hannah Pedone

data.title: I'm terrified of a market crash. Should I put $400,000 of my $1 million retirement savings into an annuity?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'We have a house worth $450,000. Our combined annual income is $125,000.'

"We don't have any nonqualified brokerage investments, and our combined annual income is $125,000." (Photo subjects are models.)

Dear Quentin,

I'm wondering what your thoughts are on putting our house and other assets into a trust. Could it help reduce taxes or protect our assets from lawsuits, bankruptcy or other unforeseen circumstances? If so, what are the potential downsides or pitfalls?

We have a house worth $450,000 and about $1 million in retirement assets held in various qualified accounts. I'd also be interested in your thoughts on annuities for capital preservation and guaranteed income.

Would it make sense to put $400,000 of our $1 million in qualified retirement accounts into an annuity that would begin paying out at age 65, guaranteeing us $40,000 a year for life, while leaving the remaining $600,000 invested in a brokerage account for capital appreciation?

My spouse and I are 55 and 54, respectively. We're both working and plan to continue until 65. We're terrified of a market crash. We don't have any nonqualified brokerage investments, and our combined annual income is $125,000.

Curious in the Midwest

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: 'Nvidia has me spooked ': Should I sell my stocks or buy real estate?

That money you invest in an annuity is no longer readily available, and you give up any stock-market gains it might have earned.

Dear Curious,

I'll outline the advantages of your proposal - and then move on to the cons.

First, the pros of putting your money in an annuity, I presume, are to find a haven for part of your nest egg, albeit at a potentially lower rate than the stock market could provide. If you moved $400,000 from traditional 401(k)s or IRAs into an IRA annuity, the transaction generally would not trigger income taxes or the 10% early-withdrawal penalty, provided the funds are transferred correctly. A direct trustee-to-trustee transfer is typically the simplest approach. If you were selling $400,000 worth of investments in an ordinary brokerage account, however, you could owe capital-gains taxes on any profits realized from the sale.

Annuities provide guaranteed income, much like Social Security, which you presumably plan to take when you reach full retirement age. What you receive depends on the type of annuity: your initial investment, the interest rate or other terms you lock in and, of course, the payment schedule. Payouts can also vary with your age, your sex and whether the product is a joint-life annuity. If you expect to live a long time, a lifetime annuity can protect you from outliving your retirement savings. The trade-off is access: That money is no longer readily available, and you give up any stock-market gains it might have earned.

Annuities provide guaranteed income, much like Social Security.

An annuity is neither a bond nor cash. It works as an insurance contract: you pay an insurance company in exchange for income. An immediate annuity starts paying within a year of purchase, while a deferred annuity starts at a later date. Money in a 401(k) or IRA that is invested in stocks can grow over time and help keep pace with inflation. Annuity income is usually fixed, so it can lose purchasing power as prices rise unless you add an inflation adjustment or rider, but that protection also comes at a price: a lower initial payout. Annuity fees can be as much as 10% of the value of your contract. Surrender charges can be substantial if you withdraw money early.

But I have some questions: I understand why the prospect of $40,000 in guaranteed annual income is tempting. If payments continued for those periods, you would collect $400,000 over 10 years, $800,000 over 20 years and potentially $1.2 million over 30 years. Make sure you read the fine print. Is that $40,000 guaranteed income for one person's lifetime? Or is it for both of your lifetimes? Does the surviving spouse continue to receive the full $40,000-a-year income? Is there a death benefit or return-of-premium provision or rider if one spouse dies? Last but not least, are the $40,000-a-year payments adjusted for inflation?

Don't miss: My wife and I are in our 70s. Should we pay off our 2.5% mortgage or invest in a stock market driven by AI?

Investing in the stock market

Third, the pros of leaving the money in the stock market: If you left your $400,000 invested for another 10 years instead of putting it into an annuity, it could grow to approximately $592,000 at an annual return of 4%, $787,000 at 7%, or $864,000 at 8%. These estimates assume annual compounding, with investment earnings reinvested, and exclude taxes, fees and additional contributions. The biggest difference between this scenario and the option of buying an annuity with your $400,000 is that the former is not guaranteed. You are potentially giving up the prospect of a larger return in exchange for security.

An annuity and a trust provide different estate-planning functions. Annuities distribute your assets per the terms of the contract, whereas a trust is designed to manage, protect and distribute your estate during your lifetime and beyond. As this guide on Estate Guru points out, trusts and annuities solve different estate-planning problems: (1) Bypassing probate or buying an annuity isn't an estate plan. (2) A trust can manage your assets if you become incapacitated, provide for minor children or beneficiaries with special needs, address the complications of a blended family and set out the conditions for an inheritance.

Revocable living trusts can benefit people with modest estates, particularly those seeking to avoid probate or plan for incapacity. For families with complicated estates, putting accounts and assets under a single trustee can keep everything running smoothly. It can also help prevent conflicts involving beneficiary designations. Marital trusts matter most in blended families, where each spouse wants to be sure their own children are provided for if the other dies. A special-needs trust can supplement government benefits, while a spendthrift trust can prevent beneficiaries from selling or using their future inheritance as collateral for a loan.

Know what you're buying, and be sure you're doing it for the right reasons.

Related: Is Social Security a Ponzi scheme? No. Don't get carried away with 1930s-era prophecies of doom.

data.title: 'Nvidia's turmoil has me spooked': Is it time to sell my stocks?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

If you are tempted to ditch stocks for property or CDs, take a deep breath before making any sudden moves

Quentin Fottrell: "I'm not convinced a spooked investor is the one most likely to make a smart move."

Investors are nervous. Again. You're not the only one spooked.

A Moneyist reader nearing retirement shared his fears: "With the market dropping so sharply, is this a good time to move some money out of investments in the S&P 500 SPX and consider other opportunities? I'm in my late 60s. Nvidia's turmoil has me spooked, so I'm looking at a couple of options."

"Real estate here in Florida seems to be presenting some interesting opportunities, with plenty of inventory and sellers who appear more willing to negotiate," he wrote. "Another possibility is moving some money into CDs, which are currently offering much more attractive interest rates."

It's a common knee-jerk reaction, and he may be overreacting. A drop isn't a crash, even when it feels like one, although we are now heading towards correction territory. The market fell sharply during the COVID-19 pandemic, and again after President Trump announced a trade war with multiple countries, including China. Both times, it recovered. And, yes, it's falling again this week amid Nvidia's woes.

The stock market regularly shows its teeth. It's the nature of the beast.

Still, I'm not convinced a spooked investor is the one most likely to make a smart move. It never ceases to amaze me how quickly people panic when the market turns south. But the market regularly shows its teeth. It's the nature of the beast. After Nvidia's earnings were released on Tuesday afternoon, you better believe that analysts have questions.

The latest roar came from Nvidia (NVDA). CEO Jensen Huang resigned last week after admitting he had been unfaithful to his wife amid reports of an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly suspect of ties to Chinese intelligence. He also reportedly had relationships with two other Nvidia employees. U.S. regulators are clamping down on a loophole that allowed the sale of AI chips to China and other countries.

After the Nvidia scandal broke, Bernstein senior semiconductor analyst Stacy Rasgon cut his rating on Nvidia's stock to "market perform" from "outperform" and halved his price target to $200 a share. Oppenheimer analyst Rick Schafer cut the stock to "perform" from "outperform" and removed his price target. Among their concerns: dependence on a single charismatic CEO, increased competition in AI chips and wider fears of an AI bubble.

Take the long view, even if 2026 suddenly looks like a glum year for equities-and go play Grand Theft Auto VI (TTWO) instead of peeking at your 401(k). Year to date as of Friday afternoon, the S&P 500 has risen 2.1%, the Nasdaq Composite COMP has decreased 1.4%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA is up 1.0%, and the Russell 2000 RUT has gained 5.2%. Keep in mind, the market has been volatile in recent weeks amid shaken confidence in AI-related stocks.

Related: Nvidia's leadership saga unfolds as demand is surging for Anthropic's IPO

Weathering storms

Nvidia is one of the largest components of major stock market indexes, with a market capitalization of $3.75 trillion as of Wednesday afternoon. Its performance is closely watched alongside that of other AI-related stocks, including Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), Intel (INTC), Micron Technology (MU), Dell Technologies (DELL) and Oracle (ORCL).

You could regard this as the long-awaited AI bubble bursting (although the AI revolution is likely here to stay). You might see it as an overdue correction. Or you could view the ousting of Huang as CEO of Nvidia as another "monster of the week," a TV trope that mirrors real-life market panics. (Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.)

If that volatility has you looking for safer ground, CD rates are reaching up to 5% if you are prepared to lock up your money for anywhere from six months to five years. CDs are better suited for short-term, safe-haven savings like an emergency fund rather than making up a significant part of your long-term investment plan.

You could choose to view these latest events as another 'monster of the week.'

The stock market has weathered quite a few storms in recent years. The more you check your stocks, however, the more apt you are to fret over the volatility, and the more likely you are to sell based on growing fear, unease, and uncertainty.

The geopolitical backdrop - the unpredictable and frankly confusing war in Iran, Russia's invasion of Ukraine and Trump's on-again, off-again trade war - has made many investors and 401(k) account holders nervous and led to fears of a broader correction.

As you move from your 40s into your 50s and 60s, the share of your portfolio invested in stocks typically shifts to reflect the time you have to recover from a major market correction and to mitigate what's known as sequence-of-returns risk.

That risk is especially critical in the years just before and after retirement. A large market decline early in retirement can severely damage your portfolio far more than a similar decline happening many years later. Ultimately, the right asset allocation will depend on your personal risk tolerance.

Don't miss: 'God works in mysterious ways': I became a Nvidia millionaire playing 'World of Warcraft.' Am I smart - or just lucky?

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Buying real estate

Selling shares that you presumably hope will see you through retirement to invest in real estate is a dramatic move. The Florida property market is as good as any to use as an example: The average home value in Florida is approximately $375,000, down 0.5% over the past year, with homes going to "pending" in around 47 days on average, according to Zillow (Z).

As the Moneyist reader points out, the Florida real estate market has fallen and stabilized, with single-family and luxury homes showing resilience. Condos, meanwhile, have had a rougher time due to oversupply and softening demand, compounded by persistently high interest rates and regulatory costs.

Stocks and real estate can both provide passive income, but are you ready to be an absentee landlord and shoulder the costs that come with it because of a bad week or month in the stock market? Good luck with those property taxes and storm insurance premiums.

You are better off playing Grand Theft Auto VI than peeking at your 401(k).

Deals exist in the Sunshine State and elsewhere. Florida's new-build construction market has remained resilient in the face of rising inventory, despite higher rates. Major homebuilders are offering aggressive incentives to buyers who use their in-house lenders. That particular trend is happening nationwide, too.

In November, 46% of homebuilders cut prices, the highest share since COVID-19, according to a monthly survey by the National Association of Home Builders released Tuesday. The average price cut remained steady at 6% for an eighth consecutive month. Meanwhile, 68% of builders offered sales incentives - also a post-COVID high.

For better or for worse - and with AI's help recently - the stock market is a beast that keeps on roaring. Over the last 10 years, the S&P 500 gained more than 230% in value compared to roughly 84% for U.S. residential home prices, analysts say, and that's before factoring in dividends or the costs of owning a home.

If you're considering a big portfolio change today or tomorrow, you need an adviser who can take a long, sober look at your allocations, age, retirement plans and goals, your investing timeline, your mix of U.S. versus overseas stocks, and your holdings in bonds and cash. All that work will take your mind off Nvidia.

Please be careful, my friends, before swapping one volatile asset for another.

Related: 'The thought of living to 100 terrifies me': Is Social Security a giant Ponzi scheme?

data.title: Here's what's been proven to help GLP-1 users from losing too much muscle from the drug
data.description:
By Jaimy Lee

People taking Zepbound who engage in consistent resistance training can still get stronger even if they lose some of their muscle, according to a new study

A new study found that resistance training can offset the loss of lean muscle mass in people taking Zepbound - and even make them stronger.

Losing weight while taking a GLP-1 medication isn't just about the numbers on a scale.

New research says that healthy weight loss with a GLP-1 drug like Eli Lilly's (LLY) Zepbound or Novo Nordisk's (NVO) Wegovy is aided by resistance training, which can offset the decline of lean muscle mass common in anyone who is losing weight.

"Although they lose lean mass, [someone] can still maintain and, in this case, even improve their overall strength and the function of their muscular system," said Jacque Crockford, a health coach and director of product development at the American Council on Exercise. That's "a really good indicator of why exercise is so important in conjunction with any kind of weight-loss journey."

The study, which came out this month, is the first to evaluate the role of resistance training in people taking the most popular weight-loss drug on the market. It showed that people taking Zepbound who lifted weights still lost lean muscle mass, but not as much as people on the drug who were not lifting weights. The weightlifters increased their muscle strength while on Zepbound. In other words, they were able to get stronger even though they lost muscle mass.

The findings also reinforced the idea that lifting weights and eating a protein-packed diet can counter the loss of lean muscle, which is a major concern for anyone who has taken a GLP-1 drug, whether that's older adults, those who stopped treatment or longevity-focused individuals.

"Lifting + GLP-1s [for the win]" is how biohacker Bryan Johnson described the study on X, while Lilly CEO Dave Ricks said, "macros plus resistance is the way." (Macros is short for macronutrients, a term commonly used by people who track their intake of carbohydrates, proteins and fats.)

About 11% of adults in the U.S. are taking a GLP-1 medication for weight loss, according to a recent Gallup survey. One of the biggest concerns about those powerful medicines is muscle loss. Research has found that people taking these medications lose between 15% and 60% of their lean mass proportional to weight loss. At the same time, people naturally start losing about 1% of their muscle mass every year starting at age 35. By the time they turn 60, they can lose up to 3% of their muscle mass per year.

Taking a GLP-1 drug when you're older can accelerate that process, according to Jeffrey Egler, chief medical officer at Noom.

"Our older populations are at risk already of having too little lean muscle to support their daily activities," he said. "They get less activity in general. They're losing muscle mass. This is one of the main reasons that we see deterioration with aging."

Strength: More important than muscle mass?

The study's researchers randomized 120 adults between the ages of 50 and 70 into two groups. The trial subjects were overweight or obese and starting treatment with Zepbound. One group maintained normal activity, and the other did resistance training three times a week. That included using tools like bands or free weights or engaging in body-weight exercises like push-ups or squats.

The patients, who weren't instructed to make any dietary changes, were then assessed using a DEXA scan to estimate the differences in body composition after about 10 months.

Both groups lost similar amounts of weight and fat mass, reported smaller waists and a lower body-mass index, and saw comparable improvements in blood pressure, glycemia and lipids. However, the people who did resistance training lost less muscle mass, which helps boost metabolism, control blood sugar, and lower the risk of heart attacks or even death, than those only taking the medication. Notably, they gained upper- and lower-body muscle strength.

"Strength is a more important outcome than muscle mass because it relates to function and frailty," Danny Green, the study's lead researcher and director of the University of Western Australia's HealthSpan Institute, said in an email.

About 20 years ago, Green ran a resistance-training program in a pediatric hospital for overweight and obese children and teens. The kids loved it, he said, even though they didn't lose any weight. However, DEXA scans showed that the participants had lowered their fat mass and increased their lean muscle mass.

When the results for the clinical trials for Zepbound and Wegovy came out, he immediately wanted to understand how much of that weight loss was the loss of muscle.

"The optimal midlife intervention for people who want to prolong their healthspan would decrease fat mass - GLPs do this incredibly well - but it should also maintain their lean and muscle mass and, more importantly, their strength and function," Green added.

For those middle-aged or older, maintaining muscle strength is key to aging well. It can prevent someone from falling or developing joint issues later in life while also allowing them to stay active in their daily lives.

Not only can losing muscle mass raise the risk of frailty, but it's a big enough problem that several drugmakers are already working on new weight-loss therapies to prevent muscle loss from GLP-1 medications. That includes Lilly's bimagrumab, which is in Phase 2 trials. Other companies like Regeneron (REGN), Scholar Rock (SRRK) and Veru (VERU) are all working on add-on therapies to take alongside Zepbound or Wegovy.

For now, however, people who are taking GLP-1 drugs for weight loss should focus on healthy lifestyle choices like eating enough protein, reducing stress and getting good sleep, in addition to developing a resistance training plan that works for them and their schedule. In the study, 91% of the study's participants adhered to the resistance training program. In the real world, it can be challenging for patients to find time to work out regularly - even when they understand the benefits.

"What we say in the field of longevity is that muscle is longevity, strength is longevity, and any personal trainer - they are religious about this," Egler said. "If you lose a pound of muscle, they think that you've lost a pound of your vitality."

-Jaimy Lee

data.title: 'Never too late to start': Practical investing advice from some of the top women in finance
data.description:
By Beth Pinsker

There are plenty of rich and influential women in the U.S. Their time may be coming.

The message is starting to get out to the next generation of women in finance.

Go to any list of the most influential people in investing and you get names like Warren Buffett, Benjamin Graham, Jack Bogle and Peter Lynch. People study their methods, devour their autobiographies and quote them repeatedly. Women rarely make the cut.

There are rich, influential women in the U.S., and plenty now in high finance and investing. It's just that few have the kind of personality-driven followings that turns them into household names and get them quoted in high-school term papers.

Jenny Harrington and Rebecca Patterson hope that their new book of essays written by some of the most successful women in finance can add these voices to the conversation. "Investment Wisdom for Our Friends and Loved Ones: Timeless Lessons From Today's Top Finance Experts" features advice on how to save, invest and make your way in the world, written as missives to their friends and families. All of the contributors were volunteers and the proceeds go to charity.

Harrington's essay, for instance, was written with the next generation in mind. She got her start on Wall Street at an investing firm - where the recruiters first wanted to steer her into sales because of her gender, but she wanted to go deep on strategy. She worked her way up until she found herself in a toxic work environment and then left to start her own shop, Gilman Hill Asset Management. She has become a frequent contributor on CNBC and one of the top gurus of dividend investing with the book, titled simply, "Dividend Investing."

Her key bit of wisdom: "A lack of investment experience is never a personal failing but rather a reality of life for most people." Her solution for changing that is for people to get educated.

Other contributors include co-editor Patterson, who is currently an independent director at Vanguard; Liz Ann Sonders, chief investment strategist at the Schwab Center for Financial Research; Cate Faddis, senior portfolio manager at Zevin Asset Management; and Susan Kasser, head of Neuberger Berman Private Debt.

Collectively, they counsel prudence, diversification and curiosity. To get started, Bryn Talkington, who founded her own investment firm, Requisite Capital Management, said not to be afraid to just dive in, no matter where you are in your life. "Be comfortable being uncomfortable. You are never too late to start - anything," she wrote.

Jamie Franco, a managing director at investment firm TCW, advocated teamwork. "The myth of the lone-wolf investor with a brilliant hunch is just that: a myth. Sustainable success is a team sport," she said.

Each one tells a little bit of their origin stories, which are not the typical country-club backgrounds you might expect of financial-industry professionals. Many of these women had hardscrabble upbringings that made them appreciate the value of a dollar well before they ever started working with traders where millions of dollars were at stake in mere seconds.

"The way I found my way to money management was that I was a cashier and I liked counting money in the drawer," Harrington said. While her family's fortunes fluctuated, she took an internship at a hedge fund and found her own footing. She attributes this rise through experience to her being able to articulate financial concepts in a way that it's easy to understand.

"Maybe because I didn't start off on third base with investment knowledge - and many of the other contributors, either - now I'm able to speak about it," she said.

That ability to communicate with others is key to getting women onto the canon of investing legends. Warren Buffett would be just another billionaire if he didn't write his regular investing letters that anyone can read, and put out his philosophies in print. Same with the other usual male suspects on the lists, from Benjamin Franklin to Milton Friedman to Jim Cramer.

"They're constantly putting themselves out there and they have these wonderful quips," said Harrington. "They're very profound, but they're also written in a way that just about anyone can understand them. It's that combination of having huge assets but also a very, very big personality."

One thing that hampered women in the investing world, Harrington said, is that many of them work for firms where compliance keeps them under wraps. When you work your way up the ranks today - there weren't many (or any) women at the executive level when Benjamin Graham was coming up - you have to play by corporate rules and that means that every TV appearance, social-media post and book proposal is highly regulated. The system is set up to discourage the quotable - and shareable - witty clip.

Sometimes there's also fear of blowback that holds people back from saying what they think. "I said some innocuous stuff on social media about Nvidia and people are calling me the stupidest person on Earth," said Harrington, who shrugged it off as probably coming from not even a real person.

These constraints actually made it complicated for Harrington and Patterson to get contributions for the book, in some cases. "You see that lack of willingness to just, you know, go hard," Harrington said.

Harrington hopes the book will encourage a new generation of people - not just women - to learn to invest and build their financial knowledge. And that other women in the industry will be inspired to tell their stories and share their wisdom.

"The scales are just so unbalanced. But when they are just a hair more balanced, I'm going to bet you that five books come out of this one," Harrington said.

data.title: One thing Thanksgiving travelers can be thankful for: Gas prices are down 75 cents from this year's peak
data.description:
By Genna Contino

Analysts expect gas prices to continue to fall through the end of the year

Gas prices have fallen just in time for Thanksgiving - and are expected to keep dropping through the end of the year.

Travelers preparing for Thanksgiving trips will find cheaper gasoline prices at the pump after months of elevated fuel prices.

The average cost of a gallon of gas in the U.S. was $3.64 Friday early afternoon, according to GasBuddy. While that was still about 50 cents higher than 2025's average, it's a significant drop from the more than $4.40 a gallon consumers were paying in May and September of this year.

Gas prices typically decrease during the fall, but fuel experts say factors beyond seasonal trends are driving the sharp decline. Resolved refinery issues in the Great Lakes region, more oil flowing through the Strait of Hormuz, tumbling oil prices (CL00) (CL.1) (BRN00) and even the midterm election results have helped bring gas prices down by 60 cents a gallon from just last month.

As a result, Americans filling up their cars are seeing significant savings. During September's peak, U.S. consumers were spending about $428 million more every day on gas compared to a year prior, said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy. That number has now fallen to about $230 million more a day.

"The declining prices now are saving Americans hundreds of millions collectively every day compared to the peak," De Haan said.

That's good news for the nearly 73 million people that AAA estimates will be traveling by car this Thanksgiving, many of whom have been turning to their emergency savings accounts and buy-now-pay-later loans to cover the rising cost of gas and groceries.

Even though prices have begun to fall, Pavel Molchanov, an energy analyst at Raymond James, noted that the price of gasoline is still up 45% year to date, while oil is up 42%.

"Without a diplomatic breakthrough, the price of oil will remain significantly higher" than prewar levels in the $60-a-barrel range, he said.

Market extra: Global oil supplies are suddenly flowing. Why a crude glut won't mean cheaper diesel.

Still, Molchanov expects prices to continue to fall largely due to seasonal trends of gasoline demand softening in the winter, even if oil prices remain flat.

"If the price of oil stays exactly where it is for the next six weeks, we should expect to see prices at the pump ending the year ... maybe 10 to 20 cents [a gallon] lower," he said.

While De Haan is keeping an eye on geopolitical news that could sway the price of oil, he expects gasoline prices to remain lower for consumers until next spring, when prices tend to tick back up.

"Gas prices just ebb and flow, but it's certainly good news, especially ahead of a key psychological holiday," De Haan said.?"Americans see these prices every day. It probably will improve sentiment on the economy to see prices falling so significantly ahead of a holiday [when] many Americans are watching the price of gas."

data.title: My husband spent $80,000 on a boat, yet says my plans for a $100,000 pottery studio are irresponsible. Who's right?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'We have $2.9 million in retirement accounts. That includes some money that we inherited about 10 years ago.'

"My husband, however, is skeptical. He says that's a lot of money to spend on something that I'm trying to profit from." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

My husband and I have been married for 31 years. He's 65 and I'm 62. I work part-time in a dental office and we have a house that's fully paid off. It's worth about $900,000. Best of all, we have $2.9 million in retirement accounts. That includes some money that we inherited about 10 years ago.

For the last 15 years, I have dreamed of opening my own pottery studio. I've taken lessons at our Saturday market for several years, and I find it extremely meditative and also a wonderful pastime. There's a space near an old rail depot, about 900 square feet, which would be perfect for a pottery studio, where I could teach others. By my estimations, insurance, equipment and rent would require about $100,000.

My husband, however, is skeptical. He says that's a lot of money to spend on something that I'm trying to profit from. My sister says it's bad timing given that we're both heading into retirement. Three years ago, he purchased a boat for $80,000 and spent $12,000 on a new motor and fishfinder. He barely used it, and finally sold it at a loss.

I'm not claiming my pottery studio will make us rich, but I'm perfectly willing to come up with a business plan and set a budget, with a red line on the amount of money I would be prepared to lose. I'd actually also start a lot smaller and build up if the price is right. We could have 30 years ahead of us in retirement, and I want to spend it doing something that brings me a lot of joy.

Am I being unrealistic?

A 62-Year-Old Wife

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: 'I like the idea of a big return': My financial adviser wants me to invest $350,000 in a UAE data center. Is this risky?

Tell your husband that you're not giving up before you've even started.

Dear Wife,

From your letter, it doesn't sound like pottery is just a business for you.

For you, pottery is a passion, and it's important to have something you like doing in retirement. If you are going to choose to open a business, it should be something you will love because it won't always be easy, and you may need to rely on that bedrock of belief when the going gets tough. That's in addition to financial projections, advice from an accountant, knowing where you draw a hard line on the budget if sales dry up, and even a Plan B for the space.

I'm not going to tell you to open a business and spend $100,000, which could be a little on the high side, although you will know more when you compare this plan to similar-sized businesses and complete your due diligence. More important, I'm not going to tell you not to do it, and I don't think anyone else should, either, at least not without hearing you out, visiting the proposed site and, crucially, seeing your business plan. What stands out from your letter is your husband's immediate, possibly knee-jerk, opposition.

However, pointing out that he bought an $80,000 motorboat and ended up throwing good money after bad and selling it at a loss may be fair, but it doesn't help your cause. Yes, he decided to pursue something that he eventually tired of or decided wasn't worth all the hassle and expense. He's the one who apparently lost interest in a project after spending nearly six figures, not you. But it won't help to trade successes and failures in a tit-for-tat argument.

If a pottery studio is a vocation, you have earned the right to at least look into it.

It may be that you don't have to lease this building, as romantic as it sounds. You could rent a space at a retirement center or local school, at least initially, invest in the equipment to host pottery classes, build up word of mouth or an online presence and see how much demand is out there. That way, you won't be locked into a lease if the demand is not there. It will also help you envision what success means to you. Is it teaching a twice-weekly class? Or running a full-time studio?

You raise a great point when you say your retirement is not about doing nothing, or spending all of your time on the golf course or tennis court, or sitting in your garden reading - rather, it's about pursuing work that fulfills you. If pottery is a vocation for you, you have earned the right to at least look into it, given that you have worked for probably 40-plus years in jobs that helped you and your husband build a $2.9 million nest egg, even if those jobs were not your first choice.

For what it's worth, your business plan should include projected costs, including the lease, insurance, equipment, advertising, branding and marketing; projected revenue; the target market (there may be schools or senior centers nearby that would jump at the opportunity for their community to learn pottery); and, of course, the competition (find out if there are similar businesses in your area and, if so, how close they are and what they charge for classes).

Related: 'I don't want to die on the sales floor': I'm 67 and earn $19.50 an hour at a big-box store. When can I finally retire?

Running the numbers

You won't win this argument on statements that your husband is the proverbial pot calling the kettle black, and you may not "win" the argument at all. But you will lend more credence to your pottery studio idea through data. You have $2.9 million for retirement, a mortgage-free house worth $900,000, hardly any debt, a husband who has already retired, Social Security coming down the pike, and you continue to work part-time, although that may have to end if you set up this studio.

To put your small business in context: Startup costs of $100,000 represent 3.45% of your retirement account balance. That's not nothing, but neither is it an outrageous, extravagant risk, particularly given that this is an investment to further a pastime that brings you joy and, hopefully, makes money. What is your annual income now? What will it be in five years? What are your annual expenses? How much of your retirement is in traditional accounts versus Roth?

Another missing piece of this puzzle: Do you have a "fun money" account, an emergency fund or CDs or bonds to draw from? Otherwise, you would have to take this money from your investments. That would mean you need to take more than $100,000, because you would have to pay tax on the money you withdraw from a traditional IRA or 401(k). You would lose future investment returns (which you would ideally recoup, even if only in part, from your studio).

A $100,000 startup cost represents 3.45% of your retirement-account balance.

Tell your husband that you're not giving up before you've even started, just as you would not expect him to give up on a passion project without at least stress-testing the finances. The unspoken part of this conversation, particularly after his motorboat project, is hanging over you. It does not sound like you are asking him for permission, per se - rather, you are requesting his support, and I assume you have both contributed to your retirement fund, either as a corporate worker or a homemaker.

Agree on a maximum amount you can afford to lose on a studio. You will need working capital, particularly in the early stages, when you are building your reputation. This is an opportunity to step back and ask what you want from retirement. How do you want to spend your savings? What kind of issues require unanimous agreement? (Did you agree to the motorboat purchase, for instance?) How will you navigate such issues while respecting each other's space?

A woman named Kyla Glendenning opened up a pottery studio in Fort Lauderdale and said she had revenue of $71,000 in the first six months, but spent nearly $20,000 on Facebook advertisements. That tells me, in addition to the costs of setting up a studio, signing a lease and buying equipment, that your biggest challenges will be getting the word out that you exist. Her online tutorials and videos on social media - where I found her - also require both time and money.

Don't let anyone crack your bowls before they've even hit the kiln.

Related: My wife says we can't afford to retire. I vetoed her $8,000 trip to Italy. We're in our 60s and have $4 million. Do I keep working?

data.title: Persona Earns CEN/TS 18099 High Certification for Injection Attack Detection
data.description:
Persona Earns CEN/TS 18099 High Certification for Injection Attack Detection

Independent evaluation of Persona's Android SDK confirms defenses against deepfakes and other injected media at the top level of the first standard

Persona, the leading global identity platform, today announced that its Android SDK has earned CEN/TS 18099 High certification for injection attack detection (IAD). High certification  is the top level of the European standard. The evaluation was run by CLR CERT, the certification body of Cabinet Louis Reynaud (CLR) Labs. CLR Labs is accredited under ISO/IEC 17025, the international standard for testing laboratories, and it edits CEN/TS 18099. This certificated injection attack detection is available to all Persona customers and can be activated by working with Persona's team.

Injection attacks skip the camera entirely. Instead of holding a photo or mask up to a lens, fraudsters use virtual cameras, emulators and tampered devices to feed stolen, manipulated, or AI-generated media straight into the verification flow. To the system, the result looks like a real live capture, and traditional liveness checks aren't built to catch it.

"Our customers are facing more sophisticated deepfakes, face swaps and replay attacks while their identity verification volumes grow rapidly," said Irfan Faizullabhoy, product manager at Persona. "Earning CEN/TS 18099 High is one way we're helping them stay ahead of both, with independently tested defenses that work at scale."

A demanding, independent evaluation

The European Committee for Standardization (CEN) published CEN/TS 18099 in 2024 as the first standard for testing injection attack detection. It grades systems at three levels: Basic, Substantial and High. To test at the High level, evaluators spent at least 30 person-days attacking Persona's Android SDK. They used at least three injection methods, including rooted devices, tampered camera services and custom operating system builds. They also used at least 15 types of attack media, including deepfake videos, AI-generated faces and spliced video clips. Evaluators checked that real users could still verify, so a system couldn't pass just by blocking everyone.

"CLR CERT congratulates Persona on achieving High-level compliance under the CLR CERT IAD certification program for CEN/TS 18099," said Kévin Carta, director of CLR Labs. "As editor of the European standard on biometric injection attacks, we built this evaluation to test defenses against injected video, tampered apps, and modified operating systems. In a constantly changing digital world, compliance is more essential than ever. We are honored that Persona selected CLR CERT."

Built for fraud teams, invisible to real users

Persona's injection attack defenses run automatically and in real time. Users take a short guided selfie while Persona analyzes video, device and camera signals in the background to confirm a live person is in front of a real camera. Fraud and risk teams get clear reason codes, such as "virtual camera detected," so they can explain each decision during audits and appeals.

"Deepfake submissions keep growing in volume and sophistication, but agentic AI is an even more alarming trend," said Daniel Lee, product lead at Persona. "We're seeing more real-time phishing attacks where bad actors mimic verification flows, trick people into submitting their government IDs and selfies and then try to inject that genuine media into legitimate sessions. That makes detecting and stopping injection attacks more critical than ever."

Meeting the EU's rising bar for remote identity proofing

The certification comes as the EU tightens its rules for remote identity proofing. The EU Anti-Money Laundering Regulation, which covers remote customer identification, applies from July 10, 2027. European identity-proofing standards, including ETSI TS 119 461 for trust service providers, already point to CEN/TS 18099 testing.

Persona's certification is listed on the CLR CERT certified products list at clr-cert.eu/produits_certifies. To learn more, visit: https://withpersona.com/blog/persona-achieves-cen-ts-18099-high-certification 

Customers can turn on certified injection attack detection by contacting their Persona account team.

About Persona

Persona is an identity platform that helps organizations keep the internet safer and more accessible for real people and businesses. Organizations use Persona to securely collect, verify, manage and make decisions about the identities of individuals, businesses and agents, with AI-backed orchestration that automates and streamlines the process from end to end. Backed by Persona’s own research into emerging threats, its fraud prevention and identity theft protection have stopped more than 300 million fraud attempts, including synthetic identities, account takeovers and deepfakes.

Founded in 2018 and headquartered in San Francisco, Persona has verified roughly 1 billion identities and is available in more than 200 countries and territories and 20 languages. Persona supports consumer-facing businesses across a variety of sectors, including LinkedIn, OpenAI, Twilio, Square, Udemy, Travelex and Gusto. For more information, visit withpersona.com.
